newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin surprises doctors with pace of recovery.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin surprises doctors with pace of recovery.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, surprising doctors with the pace of his recovery after quintuple heart bypass surgery, resumed full presidential duties on Wednesday and began lobbying doctors to let him leave hospital.

U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey said after the operation that the 65-year-old Russian leader could be back on the tennis court in four months, but he urged him to be patient and follow his doctors' advice.
"Within three or four months he could do almost anything he wants," DeBakey told CNN television after meeting Yeltsin on Wednesday.
Doctors had operated on the Russian president for seven hours on Tuesday, replacing five arteries around his heart in an attempt to give him a new lease of life.

The president delegated power to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin during the surgery and for the first hours after it but press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had signed a decree taking back control over Russia at 6 a.m. (0300 GMT).
Chernomyrdin met Yeltsin for 15 minutes on Wednesday.

"Boris Nikolayevich is active already," he told Russian public television after the meeting. "A decree was signed and is already in force. He has taken taken his powers back. This means that he is back at his job."

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was pestering doctors to move him to the elite Central Clinical Hospital, where he was treated for previous heart trouble, apparently because he would feel more at home there. He said doctors would discuss this on Thursday.
The once tight-lipped Kremlin has released a series of statements about Yeltsin's health since the operation started in an unprecedented public relations exercise.
The latest bulletin, dealing with Yeltsin's health at 4 p.m (1300 GMT) on Thursday, said there had been no complications.

"The post-operative recovery process...is proceeding normally, in line with the doctors' expectations and without complications," the statement said. "The next bulletin about the president's state of health will be on November 7."

Yeltsin has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since he won a second term in office on July 3 and his absence has paralysed Russia's post-communist development, damaging investor confidence and unleashing a new bout of political infighting.
The president's friends and foes have been waiting to see whether he would take full control or become a lame duck for his second term, due to end midway through the year 2000.

"The first thing he will want to do after he has recovered is to show he is in complete control. This is vital in a system where the president has huge powers," said Irina Kobrinskaya, an analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
But a mood of reconciliation reigned on Wednesday. Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, Yeltsin's rival in the July presidential runoff, wished the president a speedy recovery.
"He must now care more about health," he told reporters. "He must trust more of the people he is working with, otherwise there will be neither health nor government."
Russian debt prices soared towards record highs on news that the operation had been a success.

"Russia is again a buy. The best possible outcome -- of a technocratic administration under the nominal control of a convalescent Yeltsin -- is now the base case," Bank of America analyst Richard Gray said in London.
But some analysts warned that the Russian economy still faced big problems, especially on sluggish tax collection.
"I think the tax revenue thing is a big problem and it is not going to be easy to solve," said one Western economist.
"Everything that has been done in the last six weeks or so points in the right direction, but there have been so many false starts that one just has to be somewhat sceptical."
The Kremlin power vacuum has hampered government efforts to resolve the cash-flow crisis which also means millions of public and private-sector workers have not been paid for months.
